title: How do we add one sixth and one fourth?
description: Two fractions with different bottom numbers sit on one board. The lowest common multiple of the bottom numbers turns both into pieces of the same size, and then the tops are added. Keeko's doubt is that the tops and the bottoms can each be added straight away.
teaching_notes: One idea: fractions are added only after both are changed to the lowest common multiple of their bottom numbers; then the tops are added and the bottom stays. Watch for children who add the tops and the bottoms separately.

source: Add 1/6 and 1/4 using the LCM of the denominators.
video_script.why: The child can build the lowest common multiple from primes but has not yet used it to add fractions.
video_script.substitution: The lowest common multiple of the bottom numbers is the smallest size of piece that both fractions can be changed into.
video_script.anchor: two strips of equal length, one cut into six pieces and one cut into four pieces
video_script.wrong_move: adds the tops and adds the bottoms separately
video_script.fraction_reading: 1/6 is one sixth, 1/4 is one fourth, 2/12 is two twelfths, 3/12 is three twelfths, 5/12 is five twelfths, 2/10 is two tenths
maths_rules: 6 = 2 x 3 and 4 = 2 x 2; most 2s is two, most 3s is one, so LCM = 2 x 2 x 3 = 12
5/12 is bigger than 1/4 = 3/12 and than 1/6 = 2/12, as a sum should be
wrong idea: (1 + 1)/(6 + 4) = 2/10, and 2/10 = 0.2 is smaller than 1/4 = 0.25
video_script.design: Two strips of the same length cut into sixths and fourths, then both cut into twelfths. Assumes the lowest common multiple from primes. Keeko's doubt: add tops and bottoms separately.

beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; two strips of the same length, one with 1/6 shaded and one with 1/4 shaded, and a plus sign between them

marks.m1: the small title card From your book appears
marks.m2: the two strips appear with one piece shaded on each
marks.m3: the plus sign and a question mark appear

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book about adding two fractions.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We have one sixth of a strip and one fourth of a strip.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>What is one sixth plus one fourth?

beats.on_screen: the two strips stay on the board and Keeko sits beside them
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the two strips side by side with pieces of different sizes; a cut line shows the sixths and fourths both needing a common size; the words lowest common multiple appear

marks.m1: the two strips show pieces of equal size being added
marks.m2: a sixth and a fourth are shown as pieces of different sizes
marks.m3: a size line shows the cut that both six and four divide
marks.m4: the words lowest common multiple appear on the size line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We can add pieces only when they are the same size.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>A sixth and a fourth are different sizes, so we cannot add them yet.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>We change both to pieces whose bottom number is divided by both six and four.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The smallest such number is called the lowest common multiple of six and four.

marks.m1: the two fractions are written as the given

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, the two fractions are one sixth and one fourth.

marks.m1: the sum 1/6 + 1/4 is written with a box after it

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find their sum.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: LCM of the bottoms. 6 = 2 x 3 and 4 = 2 x 2. Most 2s: two. Most 3s: one. LCM = 2 x 2 x 3 = 12

marks.m2: the most 2s and the most 3s are circled

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, find the lowest common multiple of six and four. Six is two times three, and four is two times two.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Take the most twos that appear, which is two twos, and the most threes, which is one three.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Two times two times three gives the lowest common multiple, twelve.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: change both to twelfths. 1/6 = (1 x 2)/(6 x 2) = 2/12 and 1/4 = (1 x 3)/(4 x 3) = 3/12
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, change each fraction to twelfths by multiplying its top and bottom by the same number. Six times two is twelve, so one sixth is two twelfths.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Four times three is twelve, so one fourth is three twelfths.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: add the tops, the bottom stays. 2/12 + 3/12 = (2 + 3)/12

marks.m1: 2/12 + 3/12 is written, and the pieces on the strip are the same size
marks.m2: (2 + 3)/12 is written with the bottom 12 unchanged

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, add the tops, because the pieces are now the same size.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two twelfths plus three twelfths is two plus three, out of twelve.

marks.m2: five shaded twelfths show on the strip, bigger than either part

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The sum is five twelfths.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>It is bigger than one sixth and bigger than one fourth, as a sum should be.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the strips
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: a doubt bubble shows (1 + 1)/(6 + 4) = 2/10; a strip shows 2/10 shorter than 1/4; the bubble is struck through

marks.m3: the bubble is struck through and the words same size first appear

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks the sum is two tenths. One plus one is two, and six plus four is ten.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But one fourth alone is bigger than two tenths. A sum cannot be smaller than one of its parts.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Change both to the same size of piece first, and then add only the tops.
